extracted.intended_audience: general readers of translated Indian folktales / literary fiction
extracted.subtask_description: A translated narrative from the Vikram and the Baital cycle (mythic/folktale fiction) recounting stories, moral debates, and social customs. The page is a literary story rather than an instructional guideline, though it contains embedded prescriptive passages about education, discipline, and social rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for choosing a Guru/teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: They chose a Guru or teacher strictly according to the orders of their faith, a wise man of honourable family and affable demeanour, who was not a glutton nor leprous, nor blind of one eye, nor blind of both eyes, nor very short, nor suffering from whitlows, asthma, or other disease, nor noisy and talkative, nor with any defect about the fingers and toes, nor subject to his wife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a teacher according to religious prescriptions; prefer one of honourable family, affable conduct, and without physical defects, chronic illnesses, or certain social weaknesses (e.g., being 'subject to his wife' or being noisy/talkative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for upbringing/education of boys
rubrics_metrics.description: Their father sedulously cultivated implicit obedience, humble respect, warm attachment, and the virtues and sentiments generally. He praised them secretly and reprehended them openly, derided their looks, and dressed them coarsely to preserve them from vanity and conceit. Whenever they anticipated a 'treat,' he punctually disappointed them, to teach them self-denial. Often when he had promised them a present, he would revoke, not break his word, in order that discipline might have a name and habitat in his household. And knowing by experience how much stronger than love is fear, he frequently threatened, browbeat, and overawed them with the rod and the tongue, with the terrors of this world, and with the horrors of the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prescriptive regimen emphasizing obedience and humility: use covert praise, visible reprimand, material austerity, deliberate disappointment to teach self-denial, and fear-based discipline (threats and punishment) as instruments of moral formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student conduct rules at Chatushpati (prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In their rare days of ease--they were enjoined to disport themselves with the gravity and the decorum that befit young Samditats, not to engage in night frolics, not to use free jests or light expressions, not to draw pictures on the walls, not to eat honey, flesh, and sweet substances turned acid, not to talk to little girls at the well-side, on no account to wear sandals, carry an umbrella, or handle a die even for love, and by no means to steal their neighbours’ mangoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A list of explicit behavioural prohibitions for students: maintain decorum, avoid amusements and levity, abstain from certain foods and social interactions, and avoid specific outward signs (sandals, umbrella) and games (dice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily schedule of study at the Chatushpati
rubrics_metrics.description: Every morning the teacher and his pupils assembled in the hut where the different classes were called up by turns. They laboured till noon, and were allowed only two hours, a moiety of the usual time, for bathing, eating, sleep, and worship, which took up half the period. At 3 P.M. they resumed their labours, repeating to the tutor what they had learned by heart, and listening to the meaning of it: this lasted till twilight. They then worshipped, ate and drank for an hour: after which came a return of study, repeating the day’s lessons, till 10 P.M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strict, highly structured daily timetable: intense morning study until noon, a short midday break, afternoon study from 3pm until twilight, a short evening worship/meal, then further study until 10pm—heavy emphasis on repetition and memorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral classification of four characters
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four different characters in the world: he who perfectly obeys the commands; he who practices the commands, but follows evil; he who does neither good nor evil; and he who does nothing but evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A taxonomy for judging persons' moral types used by the Gurus to evaluate students and determine corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended sanctions for gamblers (governance advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Cut off the gambler’s nose and ears, hold up his name to public contempt, and drive him out of the country, that he may thus become an example to others. For they who play must more often lose than win; and losing, they must either pay or not pay. In the latter case they forfeit caste, in the former they utterly reduce themselves. And though a gambler’s wife and children are in the house, do not consider them to be so, since it is not known when they will be lost.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severe corporal and social punishments recommended as deterrence: physical mutilation, public shame, exile; rationale grounded in gambling's perceived social and economic harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice for handling libertines in educational settings
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The wise shun woman, who can fascinate a man in the twinkling of an eye; but the foolish, conceiving an affection for her, forfeit in the pursuit of pleasure their truthfulness, reputation, and good disposition, their way of life and mode of thought, their vows and their religion. ... therefore must thou too, O young man! quit this seat of learning with all possible expedition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Libertinism is treated as corrupting: recommended response is removal from the seat of learning (expulsion) to prevent moral contagion and as corrective measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment gradation for theft and robbery
rubrics_metrics.description: They warned the thief that petty larceny is punishable with fine, theft on a larger scale with mutilation of the hand, and robbery, when detected in the act, with loss of life; that for cutting purses, or for snatching them out of a man’s waistcloth, ‘the first penalty is chopping off the fingers, the second is the loss of the hand, and the third is death.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clearly tiered set of penalties corresponding to severity of property crimes: fines for minor theft, mutilation for larger theft, and death for violent/major robbery—with explicit examples (purse-cutting) illustrating escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental reformation measures (consequences to induce reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: He took the opportunity of turning them out upon the world, ... In order to supply them with a motive for the task proposed, he stopped their monthly allowance. But he added, if they would repair to the neighbouring university of Jayasthal, and there show themselves something better than a disgrace to their family, he would direct their maternal uncle to supply them with all the necessaries of food and raiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use withdrawal of financial support and conditional promises of assistance plus mandated change of environment (transfer to another institution) as tools to force reformation and self-sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of argument and evidence (atheist's debate criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: In debate he preferred logical and mathematical grounds, requiring a categorical 'because' in answer to his 'why?' He was full of morality and natural religion... He did not credit miracles because, according to him, nature never suspends her laws, and, moreover, he had never seen aught supernatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A model of rationalist critique: demand for logical/mathematical justification, empirical/physical evidence, and skepticism of revelation/miracles; positions to be refuted by inference, comparison, Sruti and Smriti, and other traditional means.
